subsystems.name: Brain mapping (connectomics)
subsystems.role: produces a wiring diagram of every neuron and synapse — the 'parts list' of a mind.

subsystems.name: Functional recording
subsystems.role: measures what those neurons are actually doing, not just how they are wired.

subsystems.name: Implant and data link
subsystems.role: would carry a very large number of channels in and out of living tissue.

subsystems.name: Computational substrate
subsystems.role: a machine able to run a full brain model in real time.

subsystems.name: Embodiment and interface
subsystems.role: gives the simulated mind senses and a way to act.

subsystems.name: Verification
subsystems.role: tests whether the copy behaves like the original — the open scientific problem.

buildSteps.title: Map a whole brain at synapse resolution
buildSteps.detail: Slice tissue into nanometre-thin sections, image each one, and stitch the images into a 3D wiring diagram. A fruit-fly brain has been done; a mouse is in progress; a human brain has roughly 86 billion neurons and is thousands of times larger again.

buildSteps.title: Record a living brain's activity
buildSteps.detail: Place electrodes or optical sensors across the whole brain and log the firing of every neuron over time. Today's arrays reach thousands of channels in animals; a human brain has billions of neurons.

buildSteps.title: Build biophysically detailed neuron models
buildSteps.detail: Turn each cell type into equations describing how it integrates inputs and fires — the same approach used in simulation projects for cortical columns and small nervous systems.

buildSteps.title: Connect the model to the map
buildSteps.detail: Wire the simulated neurons together exactly as the connectome says, then tune the model until its activity patterns resemble the recorded ones.

buildSteps.title: Run it in real time
buildSteps.detail: Simulate the whole network faster than biological time on a large computer cluster — today this is possible only for tiny nervous systems or small brain regions.

buildSteps.title: Validate the copy
buildSteps.detail: Compare behaviour, memory and responses with the original. If they diverge, the model is wrong; no one yet knows what level of agreement would count as success.

buildSteps.title: Establish a read-out path
buildSteps.detail: Only then could a high-bandwidth implant in a living person feed the model continuously, so the simulation reflects a particular individual rather than a generic brain.

buildSteps.title: Provide a body and a life
buildSteps.detail: Give the simulation sensors and outputs so it can interact with the world, and decide — a legal and ethical question, not an engineering one — what status a copy has.

prerequisites.why: mapping one human brain at synaptic resolution is far beyond current microscope, storage and compute capacity.
there is no way to read every neuron in a living human brain without damaging it.
no computer comes close to running 86 billion detailed neurons at biological speed.
research systems record from hundreds to thousands of neurons in people; this is many orders of magnitude short.
without one, there is no way to tell whether a simulation is a mind or just a very good imitation of one.

pathway.milestone: small-brain connectomes and implants that restore limited function, such as movement or speech prostheses
pathway.unlocks: tools and methods that larger mapping and recording efforts depend on.

pathway.milestone: a complete mouse brain map plus large-scale activity recording
pathway.unlocks: a test bed for comparing a simulation against the real animal.

pathway.milestone: real-time simulation of a small mammalian brain that behaves recognisably like the animal
pathway.unlocks: evidence that the modelling approach scales at all.

pathway.milestone: scanning and simulating a human brain
pathway.unlocks: the technical precondition for any claim of uploading — and, separately, hard questions about whether the copy is the person.
